Module 1.title: First & Second Laws Applied to Flow Systems, Exergy and Availability
Module 1.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: SFEE, Exergy & Second Law
  • Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE): $\dot{Q} - \dot{W}_s = \dot{m} \left[ (h_2 - h_1) + \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} + g(z_2 - z_1) \right]$.
  • Device Reductions:
    • Boiler/Heat Exchanger: $q = h_2 - h_1$ ($w=0, \Delta ke = 0$).
    • Nozzle: $V_2 = \sqrt{V_1^2 + 2(h_1 - h_2)} \approx \sqrt{2(h_1 - h_2)}$ ($q=0, w=0$).
    • Turbine: $w_T = h_1 - h_2$ ($q=0, \Delta ke \approx 0$).
    • Compressor: $w_C = h_2 - h_1$ ($q=0, \Delta ke \approx 0$).
    • Throttling Valve: $h_1 = h_2$ (isenthalpic, $q=0, w=0$).
  • Exergy (Availability): Maximum theoretical useful work obtainable: $\psi = (h - h_0) - T_0(s - s_0) + \frac{V^2}{2} + g z$.
  • Gouy-Stodola Theorem: Rate of irreversibility (lost work) is proportional to entropy generation: $I = T_0 S_{gen} = W_{rev} - W_{act}$.
Module 1.detailed_notes:
Module 1 Comprehensive Reference: SFEE & Availability

Key Second Law Formulations

Clausius Inequality: $\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0$ ($=0$ for reversible, $<0$ for irreversible cycles).

Exergy Balance for Open Control Volume:

$$\sum \left(1 - \frac{T_0}{T_k}\right) \dot{Q}_k - \dot{W}_s + \sum \dot{m}_{in} \psi_{in} - \sum \dot{m}_{out} \psi_{out} - \dot{I} = 0$$
Module 1.textbook_html:
1.1 Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE) Derivation

Consider an open control volume through which fluid enters at station 1 and exits at station 2 under steady flow conditions ($\partial / \partial t = 0$). Applying the First Law of Thermodynamics (conservation of energy) across the control surface:

$$\dot{E}_{in} = \dot{E}_{out}$$ $$\dot{m}_1 \left( u_1 + P_1 v_1 + \frac{V_1^2}{2} + g z_1 \right) + \dot{Q} = \dot{m}_2 \left( u_2 + P_2 v_2 + \frac{V_2^2}{2} + g z_2 \right) + \dot{W}_s$$

Defining specific enthalpy $h = u + P v$ and noting steady mass conservation $\dot{m}_1 = \dot{m}_2 = \dot{m}$:

$$\dot{Q} - \dot{W}_s = \dot{m} \left[ (h_2 - h_1) + \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} + g(z_2 - z_1) \right]$$

1.2 Second Law Analysis, Exergy and Gouy-Stodola Theorem

The First Law states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; the Second Law asserts that energy possesses quality as well as quantity. Exergy ($X$) represents the maximum useful work potential that can be extracted from a system as it comes into complete thermodynamic, mechanical, and chemical equilibrium with the surrounding reference environment ($T_0, P_0$).

According to the Gouy-Stodola Theorem, the irreversibility (exergy destruction rate $\dot{I}$) is directly proportional to the total rate of entropy generation $\dot{S}_{gen}$:

$$\dot{I} = \dot{W}_{rev} - \dot{W}_{act} = T_0 \dot{S}_{gen} = T_0 \left[ \sum \dot{m}_e s_e - \sum \dot{m}_i s_i - \sum \frac{\dot{Q}_k}{T_k} \right]$$

Module 2.title: Vapour Power Cycles (Rankine, Reheat, Regeneration and Cogeneration)
Module 2.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Steam Power Cycles
  • Ideal Rankine Cycle: 1-2 Isentropic expansion in turbine ($w_T = h_1 - h_2$), 2-3 Isobaric heat rejection in condenser ($q_C = h_2 - h_3$), 3-4 Isentropic pumping ($w_P = h_4 - h_3 = v_f (P_b - P_c)$), 4-1 Isobaric heat addition in boiler ($q_B = h_1 - h_4$).
  • Thermal Efficiency: $\eta_{th} = \frac{w_{net}}{q_{in}} = \frac{(h_1 - h_2) - (h_4 - h_3)}{h_1 - h_4}$.
  • Reheat Rankine Cycle: Steam expanded partially in HP turbine, reheated at constant pressure in boiler to initial temperature, then expanded in LP turbine. Benefits: Increases thermal efficiency slightly, dramatically reduces moisture content at LP turbine exhaust ($x_2 > 0.88$).
  • Regenerative Cycle: Steam bled from turbine at intermediate pressure to preheat feedwater in Open or Closed Feedwater Heaters (FWH). Elevates mean temperature of heat addition ($T_{m1}$), substantially boosting thermal efficiency towards Carnot limit.
Module 2.detailed_notes:
Module 2 Comprehensive Reference: Rankine Cycles

Rankine Reheat & Regenerative Formulations

Work Output of Reheat Cycle:

$$w_T = (h_1 - h_2) + (h_3 - h_4), \quad q_{in} = (h_1 - h_6) + (h_3 - h_2)$$

Energy Balance for Open Feedwater Heater (OFWH):

$$m \cdot h_2 + (1 - m) \cdot h_5 = 1 \cdot h_6 \implies m = \frac{h_6 - h_5}{h_2 - h_5}$$
Module 2.textbook_html:
2.1 The Standard Rankine Cycle & Limitations of Carnot Cycle

The Carnot cycle represents the maximum theoretical efficiency achievable between two temperature limits $T_H$ and $T_L$. However, implementing a Carnot cycle using steam as the working fluid is practically impossible because: (1) Isentropic compression of two-phase wet steam (state 4 to 1) severely damages reciprocating or centrifugal compressors via droplet erosion, and (2) Superheating steam at constant temperature requires exorbitant pressures exceeding critical limits ($P_{cr} = 22.064\,\text{MPa}$).

The Rankine cycle overcomes these physical limitations by condensing the steam completely to saturated liquid ($x=0$) before pumping, allowing liquid water to be pumped efficiently with negligible work ($w_P \ll w_T$).

Module 3.title: Gas Power Cycles and Gas Turbine Propulsion
Module 3.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Otto, Diesel & Brayton Cycles
  • Air Standard Assumptions: Air behaves as ideal gas with constant specific heats ($c_p, c_v, \gamma = 1.4$), Combustion replaced by heat addition, Exhaust replaced by heat rejection.
  • Otto Cycle Efficiency: $\eta_{Otto} = 1 - \frac{1}{r^{\gamma - 1}}$, where compression ratio $r = V_1 / V_2$.
  • Diesel Cycle Efficiency: $\eta_{Diesel} = 1 - \frac{1}{r^{\gamma - 1}} \left[ \frac{r_c^\gamma - 1}{\gamma (r_c - 1)} \right]$, where cutoff ratio $r_c = V_3 / V_2$. Note: For same $r$, $\eta_{Otto} > \eta_{Diesel}$. For same peak pressure $P_{max}$ and temperature $T_{max}$, $\eta_{Diesel} > \eta_{Otto}$.
  • Brayton (Joule) Cycle: Constant pressure heat addition/rejection. $\eta_{Brayton} = 1 - \frac{1}{r_p^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma}}$, where pressure ratio $r_p = P_2 / P_1$. Maximum work condition: $T_2 = T_4 = \sqrt{T_1 T_3} \implies (r_p)_{opt} = \left( \frac{T_{max}}{T_{min}} \right)^{\frac{\gamma}{2(\gamma - 1)}}$.
Module 3.detailed_notes:
Module 3 Comprehensive Reference: Gas Cycles

Brayton cycle enhancements: (1) Multistage compression with intercooling reduces compressor work; (2) Reheating in multi-stage turbines increases turbine work; (3) Regenerator/recuperator transfers heat from hot turbine exhaust to cold compressor discharge air when $T_4 > T_2$.
Module 3.textbook_html:
3.1 Analysis of the Air-Standard Brayton Cycle

The open-loop gas turbine power plant operates on the Brayton cycle, consisting of four internally reversible processes:

  • Process 1-2: Isentropic compression in rotary axial/centrifugal compressor ($T_2/T_1 = (P_2/P_1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma} = r_p^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$).
  • Process 2-3: Constant-pressure heat addition in combustion chamber ($q_{in} = c_p (T_3 - T_2)$).
  • Process 3-4: Isentropic expansion in turbine ($T_3/T_4 = r_p^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$, $w_T = c_p (T_3 - T_4)$).
  • Process 4-1: Constant-pressure heat rejection to ambient atmosphere ($q_{out} = c_p (T_4 - T_1)$).

Module 4.title: Reciprocating Compressors and Refrigeration Systems
Module 4.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Compressors & VCRS
  • Reciprocating Compressor Work:
    • Isothermal ($PV = C$): $W = P_1 V_1 \ln(P_2 / P_1)$ (minimum theoretical work).
    • Polytropic ($PV^n = C$): $W = \frac{n}{n-1} P_1 V_1 \left[ \left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{n}} - 1 \right]$.
    • Isentropic ($PV^\gamma = C$): $W = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1} P_1 V_1 \left[ \left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}} - 1 \right]$.
  • Volumetric Efficiency: $\eta_v = 1 + C - C \left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{1/n}$, where clearance ratio $C = V_c / V_s$.
  • Multistage Compression with Perfect Intercooling: Optimum intermediate pressure: $P_i = \sqrt{P_1 P_2}$. Total work is minimized and divided equally among stages.
  • Vapour Compression Refrigeration Cycle (VCRC): $\text{COP}_R = \frac{\text{Refrigerating Effect}}{\text{Compressor Work}} = \frac{h_1 - h_4}{h_2 - h_1}$. (1-2 isentropic compression, 2-3 isobaric condensation, 3-4 isenthalpic throttling $h_3=h_4$, 4-1 isobaric evaporation).
Module 4.detailed_notes:
Module 4 Comprehensive Reference: Refrigeration

Vapour Absorption Refrigeration System (VARS): Eliminates mechanical compressor work by absorbing refrigerant vapour into an absorbent liquid (e.g., $NH_3 - H_2O$ or $LiBr - H_2O$) and pumping liquid to generator where low-grade industrial waste heat or solar thermal drives desorber.
Module 4.textbook_html:
4.1 Principles of Vapour Compression Refrigeration (VCRC)

The Vapour Compression Refrigeration Cycle represents the predominant cooling technology in domestic refrigerators, commercial cold stores, and industrial chillers. The cycle operates with a low-boiling-point fluid (refrigerant) that undergoes continuous phase transformations:

$$COP_R = \frac{\dot{Q}_L}{\dot{W}_C} = \frac{\dot{m}(h_1 - h_4)}{\dot{m}(h_2 - h_1)} = \frac{h_1 - h_4}{h_2 - h_1}$$

Module 5.title: Psychrometry, Psychrometric Processes and Air Conditioning Systems
Module 5.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary: Psychrometry & HVAC
  • Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures: Atmospheric pressure $P_{atm} = P_a + P_v$ ($P_a$ = partial pressure of dry air, $P_v$ = partial pressure of water vapour).
  • Specific Humidity (Humidity Ratio $\omega$): $\omega = 0.622 \frac{P_v}{P_{atm} - P_v}$ (kg water vapour / kg dry air).
  • Relative Humidity ($\phi$): $\phi = \frac{P_v}{P_{sat}(T)} \times 100\%$.
  • Psychrometric Processes:
    • Sensible Heating/Cooling: Horizontal path on chart, $\omega = \text{const}$, DBT changes.
    • Humidification/Dehumidification: Vertical path on chart, DBT = const, $\omega$ changes.
    • Evaporative Cooling: Along constant wet-bulb temperature / constant enthalpy line.
  • Sensible Heat Factor (SHF): $\text{SHF} = \frac{\text{RSH}}{\text{RSH} + \text{RLH}} = \frac{\text{Room Sensible Heat}}{\text{Room Total Heat}}$.
Module 5.detailed_notes:
Module 5 Comprehensive Reference: Psychrometry

Psychrometric Enthalpy Equation

$$h = c_{pa} T + \omega (h_{fg0} + c_{pv} T) = 1.005 T + \omega (2501 + 1.88 T) \quad [\text{kJ/kg dry air}]$$
Module 5.textbook_html:
5.1 Atmospheric Air Properties & Psychrometric Definitions

Psychrometry is the science dealing with the thermodynamic properties of moist air (a binary mixture of dry air and superheated water vapour). Because water vapour in ambient air exists at low partial pressures ($P_v < 5\,\text{kPa}$), it can be treated with remarkable precision as an ideal gas obeying Dalton's law of partial pressures:

$$P = P_a + P_v$$
